Fish Hoek Crime: Cape Town’s CCTV ring of steel

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
It is indeed the wild west. South africa has seen an increase in crime, up from last year. That includes Cape Town. But property crime has not increased in the mother city, and that's because, according to the City of Cape Town, of the introduction of communities buying their own special automatic number plate recognition cameras – which are then linked to the City's control room. Already Cape Town has 650 CCTV cameras. Neighborhoods have installed an extra 400 hundred and that number is increasing. The City pays for the electricity of these cameras and allows them on their light poles. The system is based on the UK system. London has only 15 000 CCTV cameras but the police have access to 2 million other private cameras.

We highlight Fisheok which did not have one murder last year. We look at their model of how they have managed to get it right. One reason is that there is an enthusiastic band of people who volunteer for neighbourhood watch – and they use technology like laptops to keep abreast of movements of vehicles,tracked by these new cameras they have. They have close working associations with the local security company and the police. The main case study then will be Fishoek and we expand on the success of automatic number plate recognition which is spreading throughout the city.

Press Release:


CCTV Ring of Steel
Though this year’s crime stats showed a 5.2% increase in robberies at residential premises, and murder stats are up nationwide, Capetonians are feeling safer than usual. Carte Blanche reports on communities joining the cops in the fight against crime by installing their own automatic number plate recognition cameras, linking them to the City's control room and adding 400 cameras to the City’s existing 650 CCTV units.


Script:


CAPE TOWN CRIME

73-year-old Lorraine Lemon-Warde patrols the Fish Hoek promenade armed with a 2-way radio.

Lorraine: It used to not go for an hour without somebody on it calling in something. Cars with wheels stolen, cars with petrol stolen from then.

She is a dedicated neighborhood watch volunteer trying to make a difference and It’s the commitment of such people that the city of cape town encourages to help keep crime rates down across the peninsula. And it’s using innovative ways to achieve this. From 5am fitness classes for their metro law enforcement officers to get them into shape, to the training of 1000’s of neighborhood watch volunteers and also the widespread use of cutting edge technology.

Sounds Up: What is your emergency?

LINK: The countries most recent crime statistics make for depressing reading. Contact crimes are on their way up but one category of crime in Cape Town specifically has shown a reduction - business and residential robbery and LPR technology is leading the fight.

LPR or ANPR stands for license plate recognition or automatic number plate recognition and the technology is proving invaluable in the fight against crime in the cape. These privately funded cameras are put up on the most used routes roads leading in and out of many suburbs of Cape Town. One university study found that a staggering 85% of serious crimes involved a vehicle.

JP SMITH: I think it’s been an absolute game changer. Its been very important in that it has allowed what we all need to be doing a lot more of and that is intelligence led policing.

Manu Choudree heads up the Fish Hoek city improvement district and when he took on the job he only had CCTV cameras to work with but he was delighted when forward thinking resident of Fish Hoek installed LPR cameras in 2009.

John: As far as this technology is concerned, was Fish Hoek at the cutting edge, is it leading the way?
Manu: Well Fish Hoek was the first town in South Africa to have vehicle recognition. So that we quite proud of.

So how do they work? When a vehicle passes a camera the license plate is captured and is run against a database.

Bernard: It has to have been loaded in the first place so various people involved in the civic fight against crime would have noted a vehicle, a suspicious vehicle or possibly its a stolen vehicle and that Intel comes from crime scenes, from various sources and it gets manually loaded onto the license plat recognition user group.

An alarm sounds when a loaded vehicle or a vehicle of interest passes through one of the many linked cameras.

Bernard: This will now be an example of an alert that’s coming through the system.

A report with an attached picture and description of the suspicious car is sent out immediately via email or sms to various response agencies as well as to neighborhood watch volunteers.

Rouvanne: We've had a call on our whatsapp group that one of our members is following a vehicle, a red vehicle.

The next moment private security companies, SAPS and neighborhood watch vehicle will be crisscrossing the suburbs in search of that car. This particular case ended in a false alarm.

But up until recently neighborhood watches with LPR cameras worked independently.

Bernard: The problem with that is that the data and the Intel from that data was very scattered. There was no cohesive assembly of that or intelligent use of that data, storage, sharing of it.

And once a suspicious car left a particular superb, the neighborhood watch monitoring it, lost track of it. Something had to be done, and SA’s first LPR user group was set up three years ago in Cape Town. Bernard Shafer is a founding member and ex-chairperson.

John: Why was it necessary Bernard to form the user group?
Bernard: These days technology is key and it was only a matter of time before more and more cameras and camera analytics was starting to be used in the fight against crime.

Dedicated civic-minded private individuals use sophisticated software to connect all the lpr cameras. Now suspicious or wanted vehicles can be tracked all over the peninsula like this ford carrying a suspected crow bar gang. An arrest was made in Pinelands. Police found 5 number plates in the vehicle.

Bernard: This was a good example of where different neighborhood watches shared bits and pieces of plate information, registration plate data to be able to allow us to give vital Intel to saps.

The city has been forced to respond to the 300 or so privately funded cameras that have popped up everywhere.

JP SMITH: What happened in Cape Town is that while government was figuring out how we were going work with all these private installations. We saw the cameras up on the poles and thought, what now? Do you take them off your poles? They not supposed to be there. We decided, no, go for a policy that allows them to put the cameras up, we passed a policy.

The city has formally recognized the LPR user group and has provided a highly secure and integrated environment at the traffic management center to house servers and license plate database.
Poorer communities can’t afford these LPR cameras. The city plans to retrofit all existing CCTV cameras license plate recognition software and this will be during this year.

LPR cameras and neighborhood watches are integral to the city’s community policing program rolled out last year. To date the city has trained and equipped over 4000 volunteers in 3 years.

John: So there is a degree of cooperation between the city and the neighborhood watches but I guess part of what you have to do is to remind them that they are not the police service?
JP AMITH: Well we do a lot of training for them sot hat they don’t think they are vigilantes and they make sure they understand their limitations of their powers but you also don’t want them to undermine themselves. Neighborhood watches can do a lot.

And that certainly seems true in the coastal town of fish hoek where last year there was not one recorded murder.

LINK: With a population of about 40000 it’s a perfect example of how a good neighborhood watch working closely with security companies and the police can drastically reduce crime.

It’s the transport hub of the southern peninsula – and here burglaries on residential homes have plummeted by 20 per cent over the last year and this has been attributed to ever strengthening and well-organized 22 neighborhood watches that exist in the valley

John: I believe that you are a bit of legend in this part of the world.
Ted: I don’t know why. I do a patrol with the neighborhood watch

Senior citizens are doing their bit like 74-year-old Ted Spencer. And he is an institution in Fish Hoek especially since he continues patrolling despite being attacked by a thug last year.

John: Why re you so dedicated, why do you give so much of your time to this?
Ted: Well I find that being retired I've got the time available to do it. I used to be in the police force in Rhodesia so its sort of a natural thing to go around and see if I can help.

Lorraine takes pride that she is making a difference.

John: Lorraine what about the more serious crimes, you've spoken about keeping an eye on the smaller things and that’s important but when people experience muggings, house break ins, those sorts of things, what is your role?
Lorraine: As a cog in the wheel. When people are looking for something you'll be watch out. Have you seen them walk past, have you seen a person that looks like this going past and so everybody will be on the lookout but now the neighborhood watch has cameras and they are doing a lot of the work.

Manu attributes the drop in property crime in Fish Hoek to its effective neighborhood watch system and the lpr technology it spearheaded.

Manu: in essence what we doing is we enabling the police to utilize their resources far more strategically by having all these eyes and ears, by having the neighborhood watch patrollers out of the street. Patrolling the street. Using the cameras and the technology in the different areas. We able to give them real knowledge of what’s going on in the town and then they can react and do what they supposed to do.


LINK: As part of its ongoing crime fighting effort the city of cape town has recruited people into its own law enforcement unit. They start out as dedicated neighborhood watches and with specialized training move on to become so called peace officers.

These are neighborhood watch volunteers who go above and beyond. They city has trained up 300 so far. And this is in response to national government cutting down on the intake of police reservists.

John: So roger it must eat into your personal life, that’s obviously a sacrifice, you've had to make?
Roger: Our families kind of get used to it in one respect but having said that it also does impact on our family lives and that is why the call is so often made by NW for more people to join so that we can have the odd weekend off.

John: Ryan why aren’t you doing what normal 24 year olds are doing? Why aren’t you out at the movies, going to a pub meeting friends, why are you pounding the streets?
Ryan: Well I guess from an early age was affected by crime and I kind of of realized that if I don’t do anything about it, nothing is going to get done. You cant always rely on the permanent officers, as we know they already overstretched with the duties that they are dong and if I can do my little bit to assist them then they can focus on the bigger issues, you know, with that little bit we can all make a difference.

LINK: The city of Cape Town also has a rewards system in place for neighborhood watch volunteers. Over time they can progress to being contracted workers.

These unemployed vou8nteers get paid a R5500 stipend, are trained and drafted into a stabilization unit. . The city floods gang infested communities with them, for example Mannenberg which Carte Blanche featured in 2013 when gang violence there was at a peak. The city claims there have bought down shootings there from 1 to 3 in a day to 5 confirmed shootings. In 4 months.

When we joined them they were patrolling in lavender hill, which had recently flared up. That night they captured and arrested a resident who was in possession of an unlicensed firearm.

For Manu, crime reduction relies on the enthusiasm and creative use of neighborhood watches. This in combination with technology such as lpr cameras should become a blueprint for South Africa.

Manu: I don’t think there is any magic to it. Its neighborhood watches, tis people, its technology and its partnerships and I think that in essence is what makes it work.
